_note: Round-1 results as verified by the supervisor (every number re-run; see SUPERVISOR_LOG.md). Read by scripts/build_findings_synthesis.py to render Results/analysis_round1.html. correctedP = small-sample (bias-reduced) GEE p where applicable; adjustedP = Holm across all ten primaries.

hypotheses.question: Do operators fall into distinct types of assistant use?
hypotheses.result: One group fits about as well as two (ΔBIC 1.9; needed > 10). The two groups were unstable under resampling (Jaccard .76 and .47) and different in session 1 vs 2 (ARI .04).
hypotheses.verdictText: Not supported: a continuum, not types
hypotheses.test: Group operators on ten behaviours (card uptake, pre-emption, tactical consulting and keeping, recovery Suggest, decision time, drones committed, card previews) using a mixture model with 1–4 groups.
hypotheses.bar: Two or more groups must beat one clearly (ΔBIC > 10), stay stable under resampling (Jaccard ≥ .75 for every group), and come out the same when sessions 1 and 2 are grouped separately.

hypotheses.short: Checking cost explains the tier gap?
hypotheses.question: Does the cost of checking a plan explain why the tactical assistant is trusted more?
hypotheses.result: All three required parts pointed the predicted way: bigger plans kept unmodified more often (OR 1.76), checked less per drone, with the interaction (OR 0.70). The result depends on how 'kept unmodified' is defined.
hypotheses.verdictText: Not supported after the small-sample correction (was p = .019)
hypotheses.test: Within the tactical tier: do bigger plans get kept unmodified more often (A), get checked less per drone (B), and do the two interact (C)? Decision-level models, each operator compared with themselves.
hypotheses.bar: All three parts in the predicted direction, each with p < .05; the test’s p is the largest of the three.

hypotheses.question: On fixable failures, does pressing Suggest go with fewer abandoned missions, within the same person?
hypotheses.result: OR 0.40 [0.21, 0.79]: the odds of abandoning were cut by 60% when Suggest was pressed. But every no-attempt failure was abandoned; among attempted fixes, Suggest and hand-fixing do equally well.
hypotheses.verdictText: Supported on its own; just misses the family-wide bar
hypotheses.test: Recovery episodes the logs show were fixable: does pressing Suggest go with fewer abandonments, comparing each operator with themselves?
hypotheses.bar: Odds ratio below 1 with its 95% interval excluding 1.

hypotheses.short: Manual work explains the benchmark shortfall?
hypotheses.question: Is the bigger shortfall against the near-perfect operator in Strategic Heavy explained by manual work?
hypotheses.result: Adding manual rate shrinks the gap by only 13% (needed 50%). The gap itself is mostly one game whose benchmark run was unusually unlucky.
hypotheses.test: Per session, the share of the near-perfect operator’s score reached, against that session’s manual rate, with the game and the person accounted for.
hypotheses.bar: Manual rate lowers the share, and adding it shrinks the Strategic-vs-Tactical gap by at least half.

hypotheses.short: Bad session-1 experience explains the trust drop?
hypotheses.question: Does a bad session-1 experience with the cards explain the drop in strategic trust?
hypotheses.result: ρ = −0.05: unrelated. Card missions do not even fail more often than manual ones. The drop follows scenario order instead.
hypotheses.test: Correlation between each person’s change in strategic trust (session 1 → 2) and how many of their session-1 card missions failed or were abandoned.
hypotheses.bar: A negative correlation with its 95% interval excluding 0.

hypotheses.question: In the debriefs and interviews, do people say they prefer the tactical assistant?
hypotheses.result: 17 prefer tactical against 6 strategic, but agreement with the original coding was κ = .27 (needed ≥ .6), mainly over what counts as a 'conditional' preference.
hypotheses.verdictText: Not supported: right direction, coding not reliable enough
hypotheses.test: A second, independent coding of every debrief and interview for which assistant each person prefers; a sign test on tactical vs strategic, plus agreement with the original coding.
hypotheses.bar: Significantly more people prefer tactical (p < .05) AND the two codings agree at κ ≥ .6.

hypotheses.question: Does general attitude to AI (AIAS-4) predict taking the strategic card?
hypotheses.result: OR 0.80 per standard deviation: no effect, and no difference between the two assistants. Only an effect of about OR 2 would have been detectable.
hypotheses.test: General attitude to AI (AIAS-4, the only reliable attitude scale) as a predictor of taking the strategic card, allowing for the mission’s make-up, scenario, session and timing.
hypotheses.bar: Odds ratio per standard deviation with its 95% interval excluding 1.

hypotheses.short: Noticing the illogical card lowers card use?
hypotheses.question: Does card use fall once an operator has noticed that the illogical card can happen?
hypotheses.result: The apparent drop (OR 0.12) is produced by how 'noticed' was defined. Against a simulation with no real change, it disappears.
hypotheses.verdictText: Not supported: the planned test was flawed
hypotheses.test: Single-type missions only: card use before vs after the first time each person rejected an illogical card (taken as the moment they noticed it).
hypotheses.bar: Card use lower after, with the odds ratio’s 95% interval excluding 1.

hypotheses.short: A fuller queue pushes people onto the cards?
hypotheses.question: Does a fuller queue of waiting missions push operators onto the strategic cards?
hypotheses.result: OR 1.04 per extra queued mission. The test could have caught an effect as small as OR 1.14, and ~20 variants agree.
hypotheses.test: At each strategic decision, the number of missions waiting in the queue (relative to that person’s own average) as a predictor of taking a card, allowing for the mission’s make-up, scenario and session.
hypotheses.bar: Odds ratio above 1 per extra queued mission, interval excluding 1.

hypotheses.short: Taking a card makes a mission more likely to complete?
hypotheses.question: For the same person, are card missions more likely to complete than manual ones?
hypotheses.result: OR 0.81 [0.54, 1.20]. The test could have caught OR ≤ 0.58 or ≥ 1.73.
hypotheses.test: Does each mission complete in full, card vs manual, comparing each operator with themselves and allowing for the mission’s make-up and the game?
hypotheses.bar: Odds ratio with its 95% interval excluding 1, in either direction.
